ml-tensors.title: Tensors and shapes
ml-tensors.description: Learn to read a tensor's shape like a type, and predict when reshape, broadcasting or a layer will crash.
ml-tensors.html:
Your first ML bug will be a shape error.

You feed 4 sentence embeddings into a classifier, and PyTorch crashes:

RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (4x384 and 768x10)

The data is fine. The shapes disagree. Your embedding model gives 384 numbers per sentence, but the layer expects 768. Reading shapes fixes most bugs before they happen.

Common mistake: guessing shapes. Best practice: print them.

Shape bugs only show up at runtime, often deep inside a library. So print .shape after every step while you build.

Reshape only when the counts match. Pass -1 for one axis and PyTorch works out that size for you.

  • A tensor is a nested array with a shape: scalar [], vector [3], matrix [4, 3], batch [B, S, D].
  • Text batches are B × S × D: sentences, tokens, numbers per token.
  • reshape keeps the count. broadcasting stretches missing or size-1 axes.
  • Matrix multiply needs equal inner sizes: [a, n] @ [n, b] → [a, b].

ml-dot.title: Dot products and matrix multiplication
ml-dot.description: Learn to compute a dot product and a layer y = xW + b by hand, and say why GPUs love matrix multiplication.
ml-dot.html:
Every AI model is mostly one tiny move.

In RAG you ranked chunks by cosine similarity. That score is a dot product: multiply pairs of numbers, then add them up.

Every neuron does the same thing with its weights. A model with 500 million weights does roughly 500 million multiply-adds per token. Learn this one move and the rest is bookkeeping.

  • A dot product multiplies pairs and adds: [1, 2, 3] · [4, −5, 6] = 12.
  • It is big when vectors point the same way. That is how similarity search scores.
  • A layer is y = xW + b: one dot product per column of W, plus a bias.
  • matrix multiplication is many dot products at once: [a, n] @ [n, b] → [a, b]. GPUs run them in parallel.

ml-loss.title: Loss functions
ml-loss.description: Learn to compute MSE and cross-entropy by hand, and pick the right one for numbers, classes and next tokens.
ml-loss.html:
Your model guessed $400k. The house sold for $300k.

How wrong is that, as one number? And how do you add it up over 10,000 houses?

A loss function answers that. It turns every miss into one score. Lower is better, and 0 is perfect. Training is nothing more than pushing that number down.

  • A loss function turns all the model's misses into one number to push down.
  • MSE for numbers: the average squared error. Guesses 4, 4, 4 vs truth 3, 5, 2 give 2.
  • cross-entropy for classes and next tokens: −log of the right answer's probability.
  • Sure and wrong is punished hard: −log 0.1 = 2.30 vs −log 0.7 = 0.36.

ml-gd.title: Gradient descent and learning rate
ml-gd.description: Learn to run the update rule by hand, and tell from a loss curve whether the learning rate is too high or too low.
ml-gd.html:
You have a loss. Which way do you turn a million knobs?

A model has millions of weights. Trying random changes would take forever.

The trick: for each weight, measure the slope of the loss. The slope says which way is downhill and how steep it is. Step a little downhill, measure again, repeat. That loop is gradient descent. All the slopes together form the gradient.

  • The slope (gradient) says which way is downhill for each weight.
  • Update rule: w = w − η × slope. Repeat.
  • η too high overshoots and explodes. Too low crawls. η = 0.25 reached the bottom of our bowl in 3 steps.
  • Each step uses a mini-batch. One pass over all the data is an epoch.

ml-backprop.title: Backpropagation
ml-backprop.description: Learn to run one forward and backward pass by hand on a 2-layer net, and explain why activation functions are needed.
ml-backprop.html:
Gradient descent needs a slope for every weight. Where do they come from?

Our toy bowl had one weight and a formula we could read. A real network has millions of weights stacked in layers.

backpropagation gets every slope in one backward sweep. It uses the chain rule: when steps are connected in a chain, their slopes multiply. We will do it by hand on a 2-layer net with real numbers.

  • backpropagation finds every weight's slope in one backward sweep.
  • The chain rule: slopes along a chain multiply. dL/dw₁ = 2 × 2 × 1 × 2 = 8.
  • One update on our net took the loss from 1 to 0.029 (η = 0.025).
  • Without activations, layers collapse into one straight line. ReLU and sigmoid add the bends.
  • A ReLU stuck below 0 passes back a gradient of 0 and stops learning.

ml-splits.title: Splits and data leakage
ml-splits.description: Learn to split data into train, validation and test sets, and spot a column that leaks the answer.
ml-splits.html:
99.8% in the notebook. 0% in production.

Your fraud model catches every fraud case in validation. You ship it. In week one it catches none. Nothing crashed. The score lied.

Scores lie in two ways. You test on data the model has already seen. Or a column secretly contains the answer. Both are fixed before training even starts.

Common mistake → best practice: the random split

With 4 fraud rows in 20, a random split can put zero fraud in validation. Every score is then meaningless. A stratified split keeps the 20% fraud rate in every part.

Fraud, prices and users change over time. A random split lets the model peek at the future. A time-based split trains on the past and validates on the newest rows, exactly like production.

  • Train to learn, validation to choose, test once at the end.
  • A typical split is 70 / 15 / 15.
  • Leakage: a column you will not have at prediction time. It gives perfect scores and useless models.
  • Rare classes need a stratified split; data that changes over time needs a time-based split.

ml-overfit.title: Overfitting and regularization
ml-overfit.description: Learn to read a learning curve, spot overfitting, and fix it with L2, dropout or early stopping.
ml-overfit.html:
Training loss 0.00. Validation: your worst model yet.

You give a model more layers and more epochs. Training loss falls to zero. You celebrate, then run validation. It is the worst score you have seen.

The model did not learn the pattern. It memorised the training rows, noise included. That is overfitting. The opposite, a model too simple to fit even the training data, is underfitting.

Four ways to stop memorising

L2 penalty: add a cost for big weights, \( \text{loss} = \text{error} + \alpha \sum w^2 \). Weights \( [3, -4] \) cost \( 9 + 16 = 25 \). With \( \alpha = 0.01 \) that adds 0.25.

Dropout switches off random neurons each step. Early stopping keeps the best epoch. More data makes noise harder to memorise.

The balance is the bias-variance trade-off: too simple misses the pattern; too flexible chases noise.

  • Overfitting: low training error, high validation error. Underfitting: both high.
  • A learning curve shows it: watch the gap between the two lines.
  • Fixes: L2 penalty, dropout, early stopping, more data.
  • Choose model size by validation error, never by training error.

ml-confusion.title: Precision, recall and F1
ml-confusion.description: Learn to build a confusion matrix and compute precision, recall and F1 by hand.
ml-confusion.html:
A 99% accurate model that catches nothing

Fraud is 1% of card payments. Here is a model: return "legit". One line, no training.

It is right on 990 of 1,000 payments: 99% accuracy. It also catches zero fraud. When one class is rare, accuracy hides the only thing you care about.

The fix is to count each kind of right and wrong answer separately, in a confusion matrix.

Common mistake → best practice: one accuracy number

Never report accuracy alone when one class is rare. Print the full confusion matrix and the per-class precision and recall.

Then ask which mistake costs more. A missed fraud loses money: chase recall. A false alarm blocks a real customer: chase precision.

  • When one class is rare, accuracy lies: "always no" scores 99% on 1% fraud.
  • A confusion matrix counts TP, FP, FN and TN separately.
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP): how trustworthy a flag is. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): how much you catch.
  • F1 is high only when both are high.

ml-threshold.title: Thresholds and the PR trade-off
ml-threshold.description: Learn to move a decision threshold, predict how precision and recall change, and pick the threshold with the lowest business cost.
ml-threshold.html:
Your spam filter ate the CEO's email

Your classifier does not say "spam". It says 0.78: a score from 0 to 1. Something turns that into a decision: the threshold. The default is 0.5, so 0.78 goes to the spam folder.

That 0.78 was a real email from your CEO. Should you raise the threshold to 0.8? You will lose some spam catches. This lesson shows exactly how many.

  • A classifier outputs a score; the threshold turns it into a decision.
  • Raising the threshold: precision up, recall down. Lowering it: the reverse.
  • The PR curve shows every trade-off at once.
  • Choose the threshold on the validation set by business cost, not by habit (0.5) or by F1 alone.

ml-ranking.title: Ranking metrics: Recall@K, MRR, nDCG
ml-ranking.description: Learn to score a retriever's ranked list with Recall@K, MRR and nDCG, by hand and in code.
ml-ranking.html:
Is the LLM wrong, or did retrieval miss?

Your RAG bot answers "How do I reset my password?" badly. Maybe the LLM is weak. Maybe the right chunk never reached the prompt. You cannot tell by reading answers.

So you build a golden set: 50 real queries, each with the chunk ids a human marked as relevant. Then you score the retriever's ranked list, before any LLM runs. Precision and recall still apply, but now position matters too.

  • Build a golden set of queries with human-marked relevant chunks first.
  • Recall@K = relevant in top K ÷ all relevant. Order inside the top K does not matter.
  • MRR = average of 1 / (rank of the first hit). It rewards rank 1.
  • nDCG = DCG ÷ ideal DCG, where each hit is worth \( 1/\log_2(\text{rank}+1) \).

ml-embed-pos.title: Embeddings and positions
ml-embed-pos.description: Learn to turn token ids into vectors and explain why a Transformer needs position information.
ml-embed-pos.html:
Dog bites man. Man bites dog.

Same three words, very different news. A tokenizer turns each one into an id, and the model looks each id up in a table of vectors.

Here is the catch: self-attention compares every token with every other token. It has no built-in idea of "first" or "last". Swap the words and it sees the same set of vectors.

So something must stamp each vector with its slot number. That stamp is the positional encoding.

Three ways to stamp a position

Every modern model does it, but in different ways. The goal is the same: two tokens should "know" how far apart they are.

  • A token id picks one row of the embedding table. That row is the token's vector.
  • Self-attention treats tokens as a set, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same without positions.
  • A positional encoding is added to each vector so the slot number becomes part of the data.
  • Sinusoidal waves, a learned table (BERT) and RoPE (Llama) are three ways to do it.

ml-attention.title: Self-attention, by hand
ml-attention.description: Learn to compute softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V for 3 tokens by hand and explain multi-head attention.
ml-attention.html:
Who is "it"?

"The dog chased the cat because it was hungry." You know "it" is the dog. To guess the next word well, the model must pull the dog's meaning into the vector for "it".

Self-attention does that pull. Each token asks a question, every token offers a label, and each token mixes in the content of the best matches.

That is three vectors per token: a query, a key and a value. Each one is the token's vector times a learned matrix.

Many heads at once

One attention pass mixes tokens in one way. Multi-head attention cuts each vector into slices and runs attention on every slice, each with its own weight matrices.

BERT-base has 768 numbers per token and 12 heads, so each head works on 768 ÷ 12 = 64. Llama 2 7B: 4,096 ÷ 32 heads = 128. The head outputs are glued back together and mixed by one more matrix.

  • Each token makes a query, a key and a value with three learned matrices.
  • Scores are q · k, divided by √d so softmax stays soft.
  • Softmax turns scores into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values.
  • For "bites": weights 0.73 / 0.18 / 0.09 gave [0.82, 0.27].
  • Multi-head attention runs many small attentions in parallel: 768 = 12 heads × 64.

ml-enc-dec.title: Encoders vs decoders
ml-enc-dec.description: Learn to explain the causal mask and pick an encoder or a decoder for a task.
ml-enc-dec.html:
Two Transformers in one RAG app

Your RAG app embeds documents with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and answers with a chat model like Llama. Both are Transformers, with the same attention you just computed.

So why can't one model do both jobs well? The main difference is a single mask on the attention scores.

An encoder lets every token see every other token. A decoder lets each token see only the past. That one choice decides what each model is good at.

  • Encoders and decoders use the same blocks; the causal mask is the key difference.
  • The mask sets future scores to −∞, so softmax gives them weight 0.
  • With n tokens, a decoder keeps n(n+1)/2 of the n² pairs open.
  • Encoders (BERT, ModernBERT) for embeddings and classification; decoders (GPT, Llama, Qwen) for generation.

ml-kvcache.title: The KV cache and inference memory
ml-kvcache.description: Learn to compute KV cache memory with 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes, and explain prefill vs decode.
ml-kvcache.html:
Where did the other 10 GB go?

A 7B model needs about 13.5 GB for its weights in fp16. Your GPU has 24 GB. A short chat runs fine.

Then a user pastes a long document, and the server dies with CUDA out of memory. The weights did not grow. Something else did.

That something is the KV cache. It makes generation fast, and it grows with every token in the context.

Prefill vs decode: two different speed limits

Take a round-number GPU: 100 trillion math operations per second and 1 TB/s of memory bandwidth. A 7B model costs about 2 × 6.74 billion ≈ 13.5 billion operations per token.

Prefill of a 1,000-token prompt: 1,000 × 13.5 billion = 13.5 trillion operations, about 0.13 s. All tokens go in parallel, so the GPU's math units stay busy.

Decode: every new token must read all 13.5 GB of weights, plus the cache. 13.5 GB ÷ 1 TB/s = 13.5 ms, so at best about 74 tokens/s. Writing 1,000 tokens takes 13.5 s.

  • The KV cache stores every past token's keys and values, so each decode step only computes the newest token.
  • Memory = 2 × layers × KV heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes. Llama 2 7B: 0.52 MB per token, 2.15 GB at 4k.
  • The cache grows with context length and with users. That is what runs a GPU out of memory.
  • Shrink it with fewer KV heads (GQA), an 8-bit cache, or a shorter max context.
  • Prefill is compute-bound (time to first token); decode is bandwidth-bound (tokens per second).

ml-training-stages.title: Pre-training, SFT and DPO
ml-training-stages.description: Learn to tell pre-training, SFT and DPO apart by their data, their cost and the problem each one fixes.
ml-training-stages.html:
Same model, two personalities

Load Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B and type "What is the capital of France?". It may reply "What is the capital of Germany?" It is continuing a list of quiz questions, not answering you.

Now try Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. It says "Paris." Same architecture, same 1,543,714,304 weights. The difference is the training that came after pre-training.

Common mistake: fine-tuning to teach facts

A team fine-tunes on 300 pages of product docs so the bot will "know" them. It picks up the tone. Ask about a price and it often makes one up, confidently.

A few passes over 300 pages is a drop next to trillions of pre-training tokens. Best practice: match the problem to the tool.

  • Pre-training: raw text, next-token cross-entropy on every token. Trillions of tokens and millions of GPU-hours.
  • SFT: chat rows with ideal replies. Same loss, counted only on reply tokens. Teaches format and behaviour.
  • DPO: prompt, chosen, rejected. It widens the gap between them, measured against a frozen reference.
  • Changing facts → RAG. Behaviour → SFT. Taste → DPO.

ml-lora.title: LoRA and QLoRA
ml-lora.description: Learn to compute LoRA's trainable parameters and adapter size, and choose LoRA or QLoRA to fit a 16 GB GPU.
ml-lora.html:
A 25 GB job on a 16 GB GPU

Full fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-1.5B updates all 1,543,714,304 weights. With the Adam optimizer each one costs about 16 bytes: the weight, its gradient and three fp32 copies (optimizer state). That is 24.7 GB. A free Colab T4 has 16 GB.

LoRA freezes every original weight and trains 18,464,768 new ones: 1.2% of the model. The run fits in about 5 GB. The result is a 74 MB adapter file.

QLoRA: a 4-bit base under the adapter

LoRA still keeps the frozen base in 16-bit: 2 bytes per weight. For Qwen2.5-7B that is 15.2 GB before training even starts.

QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, about half a byte per weight. Each layer is unpacked to 16-bit on the fly for its matmul. Gradients still flow through it into A and B.

The 7B base drops to about 5.5 GB, so it trains on a T4. The price: slower steps and a little rounding noise in the base.

  • LoRA freezes W and learns \( \Delta W = BA \): B is d_out × r, A is r × d_in.
  • Trainable per module = r × (d_in + d_out). Qwen2.5-1.5B with r = 16 on all linear layers: 18,464,768 (1.2%).
  • B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model. The update is scaled by α ÷ r.
  • QLoRA keeps the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, so a 7B model trains on a 16 GB T4.

ml-quant.title: Quantization and local serving
ml-quant.description: Learn to estimate a model's memory from its size and bits, and pick GGUF, AWQ or fp16 for where it will run.
ml-quant.html:
Where did 10 GB go?

Qwen2.5-7B has 7,615,616,512 weights. At 16 bits that is 2 bytes each: 15.2 GB. Yet ollama run qwen2.5:7b downloads a 4.7 GB file and runs on a laptop.

The trick is quantization: store each weight in about 4.9 bits instead of 16. The file gets 3× smaller and a little less accurate. The math is one line: \( \text{GB} = \text{params} \times \text{bits} \div 8 \div 10^9 \).

Pick the format for where it runs

The same weights ship in different formats. The right one depends on the engine that will load them.

  • Memory ≈ params × bits ÷ 8. Qwen2.5-7B: 15.2 GB in fp16, 8.1 GB in Q8_0, 4.7 GB in Q4_K_M.
  • Quantizing stores small integer codes plus one scale per block. Fewer bits mean bigger rounding error.
  • On Llama-3-8B, Q4_K_M adds 0.18 to perplexity and Q2_K adds 3.5. Below 4 bits quality drops fast.
  • GGUF → llama.cpp and Ollama on laptops. AWQ → vLLM on GPU servers. fp16 → training and merging.

mlcap-xor.title: Step 1: A NumPy network learns XOR
mlcap-xor.description: Learn to write a 2-layer network in pure NumPy, train it with your own backprop, and watch the loss fall from 0.69 to 0.01.
mlcap-xor.html:
Four rows that break a straight line

XOR has only four rows: 00→0, 01→1, 10→1, 11→0. Yet no single straight line can split the 1s from the 0s. A model with no hidden layer gets stuck guessing 0.5 for everything.

In this step you build a tiny network with a hidden layer in pure NumPy. No PyTorch, no autograd. You write the backprop yourself, about 30 lines.

Then you watch the loss fall, like watching a CI job go green.

Write the code: xor.py

Make a project with uv: uv init xor-lab, then cd xor-lab and uv add numpy matplotlib. Save this as xor.py.

Forward pass, BCE loss, backward pass, update. The LR environment variable lets you change the learning rate without editing code.

  • A hidden layer plus a nonlinear activation function lets a net bend its decision boundary. That is how it solves XOR.
  • Forward: \( h = \sigma(xW_1 + b_1) \), \( p = \sigma(hW_2 + b_2) \). Loss: BCE.
  • Backward: the output error is \( p - y \). The chain rule multiplies by \( W_2 \) and \( h(1-h) \) on the way back.
  • Learning rate 1.0 works; 0.1 crawls; 30 overshoots and gets stuck.

mlcap-spam.title: Step 2: A scikit-learn spam classifier
mlcap-spam.description: Learn to train a TF-IDF + logistic regression spam filter on 5,572 real texts, read its confusion matrix, and move the threshold on purpose.
mlcap-spam.html:
A spam filter that is 86.6% accurate and useless

The SMS Spam Collection has 5,572 real text messages. 747 are spam (13.4%). A "model" that always says "not spam" is right 86.6% of the time. It also catches zero spam.

So in this step you measure with a confusion matrix, precision and recall. Then you move the threshold and watch the trade-off happen.

The model is classic: TF-IDF word weights feeding logistic regression. It trains in under a second.

Write the code: spam.py

Download the data: curl -LO https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/228/sms+spam+collection.zip, then unzip it. You get a tab-separated file named SMSSpamCollection.

Add the packages with uv add pandas scikit-learn. Note: the file has 5,574 lines, but pandas merges a few quoted lines, giving 5,572 rows.

  • On imbalanced data, accuracy lies: "always ham" scores 86.6% and catches nothing.
  • TF-IDF + logistic regression is a strong, fast text baseline: F1 0.939 at threshold 0.5.
  • predict_proba gives scores; the threshold is your product decision.
  • Raising 0.5 → 0.8 took false alarms from 7 to 0 and recall from 0.926 to 0.812.

mlcap-embed.title: Step 3: Inside a Transformer with Hugging Face
mlcap-embed.description: Learn to tokenize text, run an encoder forward pass, mean-pool the hidden states into an embedding, and check it against sentence-transformers.
mlcap-embed.html:
You have called embed() a hundred times. What is inside?

In RAG you call an embedding API and get back numbers. In this step you make those numbers yourself, one stage at a time.

You load sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with plain transformers. You read the token ids, run the model, and average its hidden states. Then you prove your vectors match the library exactly.

No magic left: text → ids → vectors per token → one vector per sentence.

Write the code: embed.py

Install with uv add torch transformers sentence-transformers. The first run downloads the 90 MB model.

The key lines are the three after the forward pass: expand the mask, sum, divide.

  • A tokenizer turns text into ids plus an attention mask; words can split into pieces like log + ##in.
  • The encoder returns one hidden state per token: shape batch × tokens × 384.
  • Mean pooling with the mask gives one 384-number vector per sentence.
  • After normalizing, a dot product is the cosine similarity: 0.784 for paraphrases, 0.086 for unrelated text.

mlcap-lora.title: Step 4: A LoRA fine-tune on Colab
mlcap-lora.description: Learn to build a 500-row ticket dataset, apply the chat template, train a rank-16 LoRA adapter on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and run it.
mlcap-lora.html:
Your prompt works 9 times in 10. Your API needs 10 in 10.

Your app turns support tickets into a JSON payload for an internal API. A prompted model mostly works, but it adds chatter, renames keys, or invents categories.

In this step you teach a small model the exact format with LoRA. You need 500 example pairs and a free Colab GPU. You train about 1% of the weights in roughly ten minutes.

Write 500 rows to tickets.jsonl (an LLM can draft them; you review them). Keep 50 more aside in eval.jsonl for step 5.

Write the code: train.py on Colab

In Colab pick Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU. Upload tickets.jsonl and train.py, then run !pip install unsloth and !python train.py.

Unsloth wraps PEFT and TRL to fit the T4. The to_text function applies Qwen's chat template.

  • 500 clean example pairs are enough to teach a strict output format.
  • The chat template is part of the training data. Use the same one at inference.
  • LoRA r = 16 on 7 layers × 28 blocks trains 18,464,768 numbers: 1.18%.
  • A 4-bit frozen base plus LoRA (QLoRA) fits a free T4. You save only the adapter.

mlcap-serve.title: Step 5: Quantize and serve with Ollama
mlcap-serve.description: Learn to merge your adapter, convert it to GGUF, quantize to Q4_K_M, serve it with Ollama, and measure its valid-JSON rate.
mlcap-serve.html:
From a Colab folder to an API on localhost

Your adapter works on a cloud GPU. Your laptop needs one file it can run fast on a CPU or Apple chip.

So you merge the adapter into the base, convert to GGUF, and quantize 16-bit weights to about 5 bits. 2.9 GB becomes about 0.9 GB. Then Ollama serves it at localhost:11434.

Last, you prove it works with numbers. An eval script sends 50 held-out tickets and counts valid JSON.

Write the code: merge, convert, quantize, serve

Three files and a few commands. Get llama-quantize from brew install llama.cpp or a source build.

The TEMPLATE and SYSTEM must match training exactly. temperature 0 makes answers repeatable.

  • Merging bakes \( \frac{\alpha}{r}BA \) into W, so serving needs no adapter code.
  • GGUF f16 is 2 bytes per weight: 2.9 GiB. Q4_K_M averages about 5 bits: 940 MiB.
  • The Modelfile must reuse the training chat template and system prompt.
  • An eval script turns "seems fine" into a number like 49/50 valid JSON.
